paragraphs.text: This [oolong](oolong:definition) comes from [Li Shan](li-shan:where-it-is), Pear Mountain, a high area in the middle of Taiwan whose tea gardens are the highest on the island, at roughly 1,800 to 2,500 metres. Most places put it in [Heping District, Taichung](li-shan:taichung-or-nantou). Tea came to these slopes late, in the last decades of the twentieth century, and by the 1990s Li Shan counted as one of the island's main [high mountain tea](li-shan:history) names.

Cold shapes the leaf at this height. Nights are cool and [mist and cloud](li-shan:why-people-value-it) sit on the slopes, so the leaves grow slowly, and the cold allows fewer harvests in a year. The usual tea of the area is lightly oxidised and rolled into balls, the way most [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) is made.

This lot is from 2019, which makes it seven years old. That is still young by the measure of [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), Taiwan's tradition of keeping oolong for years, where those who give a figure put old tea at somewhere between ten and thirty years.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
